region.en: Calamba, La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省卡蘭巴（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral riddle-tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 31 'Who is the Nearest Relative?', eBook #8299

summary.en: Grandfather Julian tells his grandson the tale of Josefa, whose husband, son, and brother are all caught with the Banahaw bandits and condemned to die at sunrise without trial; the capitan general, moved by her pleading, will release one only. Held a week for the answer, Antonio sneaks it from his uncle — the brother — because 'what to a woman is a husband? She can marry again... but is it possible for her to bring into the world another brother?' The old man is satisfied.
summary.zh: 祖父講述約瑟法的故事：丈夫、兒子、兄長同為班納豪山賊被捕，無審即決；上尉將軍憐其哀求，允釋一人。孫兒苦思一週，偷偷從叔叔處得答案——選兄長：『丈夫可以再嫁，兒子可以再生，可再有一個同母兄弟嗎？』老祖父滿意點頭。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog riddle-tale recorded by Fansler from an Uichanco narrator (Calamba); archival record. The choosing-the-brother situation is ancient: Fansler cites Herodotus III, 119 (Intaphernes' wife), Sophocles' Antigone 909-912, the Ucchanga-jataka (No. 67), Ramayana 6.24, and a Persian tale of Dahak's serpent.

passages.text: 'On my life! You will soon become insane with stories,' exclaimed old Julian one day to his grandson Antonio, who was clinging fast to his elbows and bothering him as usual. 'Now, I will tell you a story on this condition: you must answer the question I shall put at the end of the narrative. If you give the correct answer, then I will tell you some more tales.' Then the old man began: 'There was once a young man who had completed his course of study and was to be ordained a priest. Whenever a man was about to be entrusted with the duty of being a minister of God, it was the custom to trace his ancestry back as far as possible, to see that there was no bad member on any branch of his family tree. Unfortunately his mother's brother was an insurrecto. The boy wanted very much to become a priest, so he set out for Mount Banahaw to look for his uncle.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 31 'Who is the Nearest Relative?'; not verbatim.

passages.text: As he was walking along the mountain road, he came across his uncle, but neither knew the other; the uncle had a long bolo in his hand. 'Hold! Hands up!' shouted the old man as the boy came in sight. 'Mercy! I am a friend, not an enemy... I have come in search of my uncle named Paulino, general of the Patriots of Banahaw.' 'If that is so, I am the man you are looking for. I am your uncle.' Federico was very glad to have found his uncle so easily, and the old man took his nephew to the cave where he dwelt with his soldiers. Weeks passed by, months elapsed, but Federico never thought of going back to his mother; so one day Federico's father went out to seek for his son, found him and his uncle, and also remained there with the soldiers, never thinking of going back home.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 31 'Who is the Nearest Relative?'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day Josefa received news that the bandits of Banahaw had been caught by the government authorities; among the prisoners were her brother Paulino, her son Federico, and her husband, and the captives were to be executed at sunrise without any trial. Josefa hurried to the capitan general, and pleaded with him to release her husband, her son, and her brother, presenting the officer with some gifts besides; she pleaded so hard that finally the capitan general was moved with pity, and consented to release one of the prisoners — but one only. Josefa did not know what to do. Whom should she select of the three: her husband, the other half of her life; her son, the fruit of her love; or her brother, that brother who came from the same womb and sucked the same milk from the same mother? To take one would mean to condemn the other two to death; she wished to save them all, but she was allowed to select only one.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 31 'Who is the Nearest Relative?'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'If you, Antonio, were in her place, whom would you select?' Antonio did not speak for some moments, but with knitted eyebrows looked up to the ceiling; 'Nonsense! You cannot find the answer in the ceiling! You really do not know, do you? Very well. I will give you until next Tuesday to get your answer.' When Tuesday came, Antonio had gotten the answer to his grandfather's puzzle-tale — but the rascally little boy deceived the old man: he had sought the information from his uncle. Timidly he said he would select the brother, and gave his reason: 'What to a woman is a husband? She can marry again; she can find another. And what to a woman is her son? Is it not possible to bear another one after she marries again? But is it possible for her to bring into the world another brother? Is it possible? The woman's parents were dead. Therefore she would be right in selecting her brother instead of her husband or her son.' 'Exactly so, my boy,' returned the satisfied old man, nodding his gray head. 'Since you have answered correctly, to-morrow I will tell you another story.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 31 'Who is the Nearest Relative?'; not verbatim.

title.en: With One Centavo Juan Marries a Princess

region.en: Bicol region, southeastern Luzon, Philippines (traditional among the Bicols)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋東南比科爾地區（比科爾人傳統故事）

texts.period: Bicol oral droll; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 32 'With One Centavo Juan marries a Princess', eBook #8299

summary.en: A gambler finds one centavo and builds a fortune by sophistry: the chicken that ate his cake is his; the dog that ate his chicken is his; the iron bar whose gate killed his dog is his; the river that swallowed his bar is his — and the princess who bathes in his river belongs to him. Unable to refute the reasoning, her father marries her to Juan.
summary.zh: 賭徒拾得一文錢，以詭辯步步起家：吃了他的糕的雞是他的；吃了他的雞的狗是他的；壓死他的狗的鐵門之欄是他的；吞了他鐵欄的河是他的——在他河裡沐浴的公主自然也是他的。國王無法反駁這番推理，欣然將女兒嫁給胡安。

sensitivity.note: Bicol droll recorded by Fansler from a Frondoso narrator (traditional among the Bicols); archival record. Profitable-exchange cycle; Fansler compares the Cullaka-setthi-jataka (No. 4) and Grimm's Hans in Luck family, and judges the Filipino version old and likely native.

passages.text: In ancient times, in the age of foolishness and nonsense, there lived a poor gambler, all alone in the world: he had no parents, relatives, wife, or children. What little money he had he spent on cards or cock-fighting; every time he played he lost, so he would often pass whole days without eating, going around the town begging like a tramp. At last he determined to leave the village to find his fortune. One day, without a single cent in his pockets, he set out on his journey, and as he was lazily wandering along the road he found a centavo and picked it up. When he came to the next village he bought with his coin a small native cake, ate only a part of it, wrapped the rest in a piece of paper, and put it in his pocket; then he sat down by a little shop to rest and fell asleep.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 32 'With One Centavo Juan marries a Princess'; not verbatim.

passages.text: As he was lying on the bench asleep, a chicken came along, and, seeing the cake projecting from his pocket, pecked at it and ate it up; tickled by the bird's beak, the tramp woke up and immediately seized the poor creature. The owner claimed the chicken, but Juan would not give it up, on the ground that it had eaten his cake; indeed, he argued so well that he was allowed to walk away, taking the chicken with him. Scarcely had he gone a mile when he came to another village; there he took a rest in a barber-shop and fell asleep again, and soon a dog came in and began to devour his chicken. Awakened by the poor bird's squawking, Juan jumped up and caught the dog still munching its prey; in spite of the barber's protest and his refusal to give up his dog, Juan seized it and carried it away with him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 32 'With One Centavo Juan marries a Princess'; not verbatim.

passages.text: He proceeded on his journey until he came to another village; passing by a small house he felt thirsty, so he decided to go in and ask for a drink, tying his dog to the gate. When he came out again he found his dog lying dead, the iron gate on top of him — evidently, in its struggles to get loose, the animal had pulled the gate over. Without a word Juan pulled off one of the iron bars from the gate and took it away with him; when the owner shouted after him, Juan said, 'The bar belongs to me, for your gate killed my dog.' When Juan came to a wide river he sat down on the bank to rest, and while he was sitting there he began to play with his iron bar, tossing it up into the air and catching it as it fell; once he missed, and the bar fell into the river and was lost. 'Now, river,' said Juan, 'since you have taken my iron bar, you belong to me. You will have to pay for it.' So he sat there all day, watching for people to come along and bathe.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 32 'With One Centavo Juan marries a Princess'; not verbatim.

passages.text: It happened by chance that not long after, the princess came to take her bath. When she came out of the water, Juan approached her and said, 'Princess, don't you know that this river is mine? And, since you have touched the water, I have the right to claim you.' 'How does it happen that you own this river?' said the astonished princess. 'Well, princess, it would tire you out to hear the story of how I acquired this river; but I insist that you are mine.' Juan persisted so strongly that at last the princess said she was willing to leave the matter to her father's decision; on hearing Juan's story, and after having asked him question after question, the king was greatly impressed with his wonderful reasoning and wit, and, as he was unable to offer any refutation for Juan's argument, he willingly married his daughter to Juan.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 32 'With One Centavo Juan marries a Princess'; not verbatim.

region.en: Pagsanjan, La Laguna, Luzon, Philippines (narrator's home town)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋內湖省帕桑漢（敘述者故鄉）

texts.period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 33a 'The Three Humpbacks', eBook #8299

summary.en: Badly treated Pablo marries out and prospers; his gambler brothers, ruined, beg at his wife's door and are hidden in two trunks when Pablo returns. Forgotten, they suffocate; the wife pays a neighbor five pesos to bury 'one brother-in-law,' then shows him another each time he returns for his pay — until, digging a grave under water for the last, he meets a live humpback carrying fish from the fishery and kills the 'corpse that will not stay buried': her own husband.
summary.zh: 受盡苛待的帕布洛成婚自立、生活安穩；敗光的兄長上門乞食，被藏進兩口衣箱，竟窒息而死。主婦以五比索僱鄰人埋『一位內兄』，此人每回討錢都見『屍體復活』，埋了又埋——最後在水下掘墓埋葬，歸途卻遇見一個挑魚回家的活駝背，一刀結果這『屢埋不起的屍身』——正是她的丈夫。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Cordero narrator (heard from her washerwoman); archival record. Fansler finds the nearest parallel in Straparola 5:3 and the Seven Wise Masters family; 'Thus Marta tried to deceive, but she was the one who was deceived.'

passages.text: Pablo was badly treated by his older brothers Pedro and Juan: the coarsest food was given to him, his clothes were ragged, he slept on the floor while his two brothers had very comfortable beds — in fact, he was deprived of every comfort and pleasure. In the course of time this unfortunate youth fell in love with a well-to-do girl, and after a four-years engagement they were married; thus Pablo was separated from his brothers, to their great joy. Pedro and Juan now began spending their money lavishly on trifles and learned how to gamble, while Pablo was living happily and out of want with his wife Marta, going every morning to fish, for his wife owned a large fishery.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 33 'The Three Humpbacks'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day, as Pablo was just leaving the house at the usual hour to go fishing, he said to his wife, 'Wife, if two humpbacks like myself ever come here, do not admit them. As you know, they are my brothers, and they used to treat me very badly.' That very afternoon Pedro and Juan came to pay their brother a visit and begged Marta to give them some food, for they were starving: they had squandered all their money. Marta was so impressed by the wretched appearance of her brothers-in-law that she admitted them despite her husband's prohibition, and gave them a dinner. When they had finished eating she said, 'It is now time for my husband to come home. He may take vengeance on you for your past unkindness to him, if he finds you here, so I'll hide you in two separate trunks. You stay there till to-morrow morning, and I'll let you out when my husband is gone again.' She had scarcely locked the trunks when Pablo entered; he did not find out that his brothers had been there.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 33 'The Three Humpbacks'; not verbatim.

passages.text: The next morning Pablo went to his work as usual; Marta had so much to do about the house that day that she forgot all about Pedro and Juan, and the poor boys, deprived of air and food, died inside the trunks. Not until two days later did Marta think of the two humpbacks; she ran and opened the trunks and found their dead bodies inside. Her next thought was how to dispose of them. She called her neighbor and asked him to come bury one of her brothers-in-law who had just died in her house, promising to pay him five pesos when he came back from his work. The neighbor lifted the heavy body of Pedro, carried it away to a far place, dug a hole waist deep, put the corpse into it, and covered it up; then he hastened back to Marta: 'Madam, I have buried the dead man in a very deep grave.' 'No, you have not,' said Marta. 'What is that lying over there?' — and she pointed to the corpse of Juan.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 33 'The Three Humpbacks'; not verbatim.

passages.text: 'That's very strange!' exclaimed the neighbor, scratching his head. 'You are very artful,' he said to the dead body of Juan; angry now, for he had not yet received his pay, he bore the corpse of Juan to the seashore, got a banca, and dug a very deep grave beneath the water: 'If you can come out of this place, you are the wisest person in the world.' Then he returned to Marta's house — and on his way back he happened to look behind him, when he saw, to his great surprise, the humpback following him, carrying some fish. He gazed at him; and when he saw that he resembled exactly the corpse that he had just buried, he said, 'So you have come out of the grave again, have you, you naughty humpback!' And with these words he killed the humpback that very instant. This humpback was Marta's husband returning home from the fishery. Thus Marta tried to deceive, but she was the one who was deceived.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 33 'The Three Humpbacks'; not verbatim.

region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋馬尼拉（敘述者居地）

texts.period: Tagalog oral tale; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 33b 'The Seven Humpbacks', eBook #8299

summary.en: Seven look-alike humpback brothers; one marries and supports the other six, until his stingy wife, hating the burden, murders all six while her husband is away and cheats the grave-digger into burying corpse after 'resurrected' corpse — until, meeting the married humpback riding home, he strikes down 'the same man he had buried so many times before,' and the wicked woman dies of a broken heart when she learns it was her very husband.
summary.zh: 七個相貌酷似的駝背兄弟；一人娶妻供養其餘六人。慳吝的妻子厭其負擔，趁丈夫外出殺害六位內兄，又哄騙掘墓人：『埋不牢便不付錢』——一具又一具『死而復生』的屍體。埋到第六具時，騎馬歸家的丈夫迎面而來；掘墓人一鋤下去——『原來你就是那個總能爬出墳墓的傢伙！』惡婦得知殺的是親夫，心碎而亡。

sensitivity.note: Tagalog folktale recorded by Fansler from a Reyes narrator (Manila); archival record. Companion to The Three Humpbacks; the Pampango variant 'The Seven Hunchbacked Brothers' (Vitug) is nearly identical.

passages.text: Once there lived seven brothers who were all humpbacks and who looked very much alike. Ugly as these humpbacks were, still there was a lady who fell in love with one of them and married him; this lady, however, though she loved her husband well, was a very stingy woman. Finally the time came when the unmarried humpbacks had to depend on the other one for food; naturally this arrangement was very displeasing to the wife, and in time her hate grew so intense that she planned to kill all her brothers-in-law.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 33 'The Seven Humpbacks'; not verbatim.

passages.text: One day, when her husband was away on business, she murdered the six brothers. Next she hired a man to come and bury a corpse, telling him of only one corpse because she wanted to deceive the man. When he had buried one of the bodies he came back to get paid for his work; the woman, before he had time to speak, began to reproach him for not burying the man in the right place: 'See here! You did not do your work well. Go and bury the body again. Remember that I will not pay you until you have buried the man so that he stays under the earth.' The man took the second corpse and buried it; but when he returned, there it was again. And so on: he repeated the operation until he thought that he had buried the same corpse six times.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 33 'The Seven Humpbacks'; not verbatim.

passages.text: But after the sixth, the last humpback, had been buried, the married humpback came home from his work. When the grave-digger saw this other humpback, he immediately seized and killed him, thinking he was the same man he had buried so many times before. When the wicked woman knew that her very husband had been killed, she died of a broken heart.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 33 'The Seven Humpbacks'; not verbatim.

title.en: Respect Old Age: The Half-Blanket and the Wooden Plate

region.en: Malabon, Rizal, and Mangaldan, Pangasinan, Luzon, Philippines (two tellings)
region.zh: 菲律賓呂宋黎薩省馬拉翁與邦阿西楠省曼加爾丹（兩則講述）

texts.period: Tagalog and Pangasinan oral exempla; collected by D. S. Fansler, published 1921

source.work: Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 34a 'Respect Old Age' and 34b 'The Golden Rule', eBook #8299

summary.en: Two Filipino tellings of the old-age exemplum: forced on a rainy morning to send his eighty-year-old father to a farm hut, the boy cuts the carrying-blanket in two — 'When you grow old, I will leave you in a hut, and give you this half' — and the father recalls the order; and in Pangasinan, the son who must eat from a wooden plate because his trembling hands break the china begins carving boards 'for you and my mother when you are old,' and the father weeps and seats the old man at the table again.
summary.zh: 兩則菲律賓孝道故事：雨晨被迫送八十歲老父去農舍的父親，見兒子把毯子剪成兩半——『您老了，我就用這半條送您去小屋』——連忙召回祖父；另一則裡，因老人手抖摔盤而被罰用木盤吃飯的孩子，竟在屋下雕起木板：『給您和媽媽老了用』——父親流淚，從此老人重上飯桌。

sensitivity.note: Two related exempla recorded by Fansler from an Ignacio narrator (Malabon, Rizal) and a Serafica narrator (Mangaldan, Pangasinan); archival record. A Pampango variant ('The Old Man, his Son, and his Grandson' with the rope 'to have it ready when your turn comes') was printed by H. E. Fansler. Known in many countries.

passages.text: Once there lived a poor man who had to support his family: a hot-headed wife who predominated over the will of her husband, a small boy of ten, and an old man of eighty, the boy's grandfather. The old man could no longer work because of his feebleness, and was the cause of many quarrels between the husband and wife, though he was loved by their son. One rainy morning the husband was forced by his wife to send his father away; he called his son and ordered him to carry a basket full of food and also a blanket, telling the boy they were to leave the old man in a hut on their farm some distance away. The boy wept and protested against this harsh treatment of his grandfather, but in vain; he then cut the blanket into two parts, and when he was asked to explain his action, he said to his father, 'When you grow old, I will leave you in a hut, and give you this half of the blanket.' The man was astonished, hurriedly recalled his order concerning his father, and thereafter took good care of him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 34 'Respect Old Age'; not verbatim.

passages.text: A long time ago there lived in a town a couple who had a son, and the father of the husband lived with his son and daughter-in-law happily for many years; but when he grew very old he became very feeble, and every time he ate at the table he always broke a plate, because his hands trembled so. The old man's awkwardness soon made his son angry, and one day he made a wooden plate for his father to eat out of; the poor old man had to eat all his food from this wooden plate.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 34 'The Golden Rule'; not verbatim.

passages.text: When the grandson noticed what his father had done, he took some tools and went down under the house, and there took a piece of board and began to carve it. When his father saw him and said, 'What are you doing, son?' the boy replied, 'Father, I am making wooden plates for you and my mother when you are old.' As the son uttered these words, tears gushed from the father's eyes; from that time on, the old man was always allowed to eat at the table with the rest of the family, nor was he made to eat from a wooden plate. Moral: Do unto others as you want them to do unto you.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Dean S. Fansler, Filipino Popular Tales (1921), Tale 34 'The Golden Rule'; not verbatim.
